generation.focus: What Ply is, who uses it, and what it produces

__diagram__.text: The whole-project map at maximum altitude. The core loop (§1) is what Ply exists to close: declared claims routed through cargo ply to checking engines, back as verdicts and counterexamples an agent repairs code against. The watermark (§7.2) bounds what that declarative layer can ever say — declarative stratum, then the watermark itself, then the unspecifiable floor. The artifacts group shows the project's actual current state: SPEC.md is the normative design; .archi/ diagrams and tours it; tools/render proves the §7.1 visual grammar is total; vetting/ scenarios (001–004) and TODO.md's running review findings both feed back into spec amendments. Unlike an earlier version of this diagram, the pipeline is no longer aspirational: cargo ply (crates/ply-cli) now has six real subcommands, and the Kani/fuzz/mutate engines it drives are real, working adapters, not a plan. See the separate 'Ply and the Processes It Spawns' concurrency diagram for exactly how it runs them.

claims.text: The declarative source of every claim: ply.yaml (components, edges, capabilities, checks) plus inline #[ply::requires]/#[ply::ensures] attributes on functions (§5, §5.1). This is the only stratum Ply ever writes to — everything below the watermark is verified, never declared (§7.2).

cargoply.text: The cargo-ply binary (crates/ply-cli), with six subcommands: render (draw ply.yaml as SVG — needs only the declaration file, not code), check (validate ply.yaml and the anchors it points at), audit (list what a codebase's evidence rests on, and what Ply never checks), worklist (list unresolved markers and assumed contracts still owed evidence), verify (run the checking engines and write counterexample tests), and clean-views (remove older published visual runs). It has no checking logic of its own — it drives config load, anchor resolution, extraction, and engine dispatch in order (§6).

engines.text: External checking tools driven as subprocesses and never re-implemented: rustc/cargo (build), Kani (the `bounded` check), a generated proptest-based test harness run via `cargo test` (the `fuzz` check), and cargo-mutants (the `mutate` check). Verus (the `prove` check) is named in the schema but not built yet (M7) — declaring it today reports a missing-engine warning, never a failure. Ply is glue and UX over these engines, never a solver (§1, §3).

verdicts.text: The evidence a function's passing checks earned — tested, fuzzed(n), bounded(k), proved — aggregated worst-of up the node tree (D6, §7). Every falsified executable claim carries a concrete counterexample, the single finding that moves agent repair success from ~0% to ~80% (§1 finding 2).

agent.text: The coding agent or developer that reads a counterexample and repairs the code or tightens the claim, closing the generate→check→repair loop this project is built around (§1 findings 1–2).

declarative.text: Stratum 1: everything ply.yaml and the attributes express — components, edges, capabilities, contracts, checks. Fully drawable per the §7.1 visual grammar, and fully checkable (§7.2).

watermark.text: Stratum 2, the mark itself: a function's signature plus its contract, where declaration stops. Movable only downward — mode: synth lets the model write the body down from the mark, with the check pipeline holding the line (D8, §5.7, §7.2).

floor.text: Stratum 3: the imperative interior of Rust — algorithms, loop bodies, data-structure manipulation — that no grammar will ever express. Ply verifies below the watermark; it never specifies the floor itself (§7.2).

spec.text: The normative design the implementing agent reads before writing any code: terminology, toolchain, ply.yaml format, CLI, zoom model, result JSON, and the accretive milestone plan (§0, §10).

archi.text: The .archi/ bundle: named diagrams (overview, architecture, verify-pipeline, verdict-model, and tools-today) plus a guided tour of comments and reading-order steps, exportable as the standalone docs/ply-tour.html walkthrough.

render.text: A minimal ply.yaml → SVG renderer with no GUI, existing solely to prove the §7.1 visual grammar is total — every construct drawable, nothing undrawable admitted. A spec-validation tool, not the future canvas (§7.1).

vetting.text: Four scenarios (001–004) that stress the grammar and the tool, each written up with what held and what broke. 001 (an SPSC ring) found three grammar gaps that became spec amendments: no way to record externally-verified properties, generics breaking checkability, an over-broad example rule. 002 (a market-data ingest pipeline) exercised architecture-tier edges, deny rules, capability containment, modular composition (D5), and the first use of `old()`. 003 (a trading system) nested a whole scenario inside one component and used dotted cross-component references, the first real stress on aggregation and the zoom model. 004 (a new feature beside an old codebase) was the first scenario run against the real `cargo ply verify` rather than reasoned about on paper — a fragment-first design testing whether the boundary between checkable new code and unchecked old code produces an honest verdict.

todo.text: The project's running list of what's agreed but not yet done, ticked off with a commit hash the moment it lands. It is also where a finished review's findings about the tool itself get written down, including honest gaps left open on purpose — and those findings are exactly what turns into the next spec amendment.

generation.focus: System components and dependency/data-flow edges for Ply per SPEC.md §3 (Toolchain) and §4 (Repository layout): the three crates, the external engines as subprocess dependencies, and the key artifacts. No code exists yet; nodes are planned and left unanchored (files: []).

__diagram__.text: Ply is glue + UX over existing checking engines, never a solver (§1). Three crates: ply-attrs (proc macros, §3), ply-core (config/model/extract/arch/engines/harness/diag modules, §4), ply-cli (cargo-ply binary, §4/§6). Engines run as subprocesses, version-detected at startup; a missing engine downgrades affected checks (W0110/engine-missing) but never fails the run (§3). No code exists yet — all nodes are planned and left unanchored.

attrs.text: Provides #[ply::requires]/#[ply::ensures]/#[ply::pure]/#[ply::allow]/#[ply::derived] and ply::unresolved!(id, note). requires/ensures re-emit the annotated function unchanged plus cfg_attr(kani, kani::requires/ensures) — the real function is instrumented, never a copy (D2, §3).

g-attrs.text: The proc-macro crate. Its only job is turning #[ply::requires]/#[ply::ensures] into cfg_attr(kani, ...) on the real function — plain cargo build is unaffected (D2, §3).

g-core.text: The verification pipeline: config loading, the component/claim model, fact extraction, architecture rules, engine dispatch, harness codegen, and diagnostic assembly (§4). Everything between reading ply.yaml and emitting the JSON envelope lives here.

g-cli.text: The cargo-ply binary users and agents actually invoke; it wires the ply-core pipeline to subcommands and the --json envelope (§4, §6, §8).

g-engines.text: The external tools Ply drives as subprocesses and never re-implements — rustc/cargo, Kani, proptest, cargo-mutants, and the optional Verus/Miri (§3). Ply is glue and UX over these, never a solver (§1).

g-artifacts.text: Generated and persisted data the pipeline produces or consumes: the ply.yaml/schema input, the committed ply.lock fingerprints, generated harness code, rendered counterexample tests, and the JSON result envelope.

extract.text: trait Extractor + syn backend: item index, call graph, caps, contract harvest, anchors. syn does no name resolution or macro expansion, so item-tier facts are approximate — every unresolved call site is counted and reported, never silently dropped (D11, W0312, §5.3).

arch.text: Two tiers (D4): crate-tier from cargo metadata is exact and default-deny (errors A0401/A0405); item-tier from syn is approximate and advisory by default, upgraded to errors under a component's strict: true (A0402–A0407).

harness.text: Codegen: in-crate Kani proof modules (cfg(kani)-gated, sees private items), proptest suites under target/ply/fuzz/, and rendered ply_cex_* tests. Uses plain format-string templates (templates/), not a parser of our own (§4).

kani.text: Version pinned in ply.toml and recorded in every fingerprint (D9, D14). stub_verified(g) is only used when g itself passed a Kani contract proof this run in the same crate; any weaker case verifies against an assumed contract and marks the caller conditional (D5, §5.5).

plylock.text: A committed file of results Ply already earned, so an unchanged function is not re-checked every run. Each entry stores a fingerprint of everything the result depended on: a hash of the function's own tokens, the contract text it was checked against, the contracts of everything it calls, and the engine's name, version and flags (D14). A stored result is used only if that fingerprint still matches at the moment of use; otherwise it is thrown away and re-earned. CORRECTION, 2026-09-02: an earlier version of this note described a `W0302 claim may be stale` warning, a `cargo ply accept` command and an `E0303` code. None of the three exist. The spec rules them out by design (The-Ply-Spec.md around line 594) and crates/ply-core/src/registry.rs says so in as many words, because a claim is never left in the state of "recorded but possibly no longer true" that those would manage. Verified in the code: crates/ply-core/src/record.rs.

envelope.text: { command, ply_version, root: <node tree §7>, diagnostics: [<Diagnostic>] }. Additive changes only after M3; tests/ui goldens are the contract (§8).

diag.text: One Diagnostic schema for all engines: code, severity, phase, engine, check, node_id, content_hash, span, counterexample, assumptions, fixes, open_item (§8). Adapters never pass engine stderr/stdout through raw — parsed, or X0901 with raw output attached.

cli.text: The `cargo-ply` binary and a newcomer's actual entry point: check | verify | tree | worklist | audit | accept | synth | skill (§4, §6). Every subcommand emits the same JSON envelope under --json (§8), which is the agent-facing surface.

plyyaml.text: User-authored claims in the target workspace. Its grammar is fixed by ply.schema.json, which is Ply's own source: embedded in the binary, authoritative at runtime, and never read from the target workspace — an on-disk copy is read-only reference for IDE tooling (SPEC.md §5). The grammar evolves only through Ply releases and the `ply:` version field.

cfg.text: Loads and merges every ply.yaml / *.ply.yaml file in the workspace (lexicographic order, target/ and gitignored paths excluded) and validates the merged document against the normative JSON Schema (§5, §5.1). Malformed input is reported as E0201–E0203 with a JSON-pointer-to-line mapping, never an opaque parse failure.

model.text: Holds the parsed components, fn claims, anchors, node IDs, and verdicts (§4). Also owns two behaviours core to a verify run: resolving anchors to real code items (§5.2) and ordering verification callees-before-callers over the call graph (§5.5).

targetply.text: Everything Ply generates and owns under target/ply/: in-crate Kani proof modules, proptest harness crates, and Verus translations (§4, §6). cargo ply verify deletes generated artifacts whose claims no longer exist.

engines.text: Defines trait Engine { plan, run, parse } and one adapter per external tool (§3, §4). Each engine is version-detected as a subprocess at startup; a missing engine downgrades only the checks that need it (W0110/engine-missing) and never fails the run (§3).

rustc.text: Ground truth for the crate-tier architecture facts: cargo metadata gives the exact crate dependency graph (D4), and cargo check --message-format=json is the baseline build/type/borrow check every other engine builds on (§3).

proptest.text: Runs the fuzz(n) check: a generated proptest harness under target/ply/fuzz/ exercises the function on n (default 256) generated inputs with shrinking on, using requires as a rejection filter (§5.4c). A failing case becomes the fuzzed(n) verdict's counterexample.

mutants.text: Runs the mutate check: cargo mutants --re <fn> plants small bugs in the function and checks whether the same-list test/fuzz checks kill them (D12). A surviving mutant is reported as a weak spec (W0502), not a pass.

verus.text: Optional prove check (M7): translates the supported spec subset to Verus for an unbounded, no-loop-bound proof (proved verdict), in exchange for a restricted language fragment and more annotation work. Not started without its own ADR justifying the translation cost (§3, milestone M7).

miri.text: Optional undefined-behavior check for unsafe Rust (cargo +nightly miri test), landing at M7 alongside Verus. Like every engine, its absence just downgrades the checks that depend on it rather than failing the run (§3).

cextests.text: Rendered counterexamples that pass as ordinary cargo test targets, named ply_cex_* (§4, §6, D7). Only emitted when Kani's failing input can be rendered as stable Rust source; otherwise the diagnostic says so (W0541) rather than fabricating one.

__diagram__.text: Verification is modular: Ply checks every function against its own contract, and checks callers against callees' contracts, never their bodies (§1 finding 3). Verification runs callees-before-callers over the call graph (§5.5). A missing engine downgrades the affected checks (W0110/engine-missing) without failing the run (§3).

kani.text: stub_verified(g) only when g passed its own Kani contract proof this run in the same crate; otherwise f verifies against g's assumed contract and f's verdict is marked conditional (W0511), listing the assumption (D5, §5.5).

lock.text: Fingerprint = item token-stream hash + merged contract text + callee contract hashes + engine name/version/flags + active features + target triple (D14). Mismatch on any part → status stale, diagnostic W0302.

cex.text: Kani playback data is always stored (exact, engine-version-bound). The ordinary #[test] rendering is added only when the inputs can be rendered as stable Rust source; otherwise the diagnostic says so (W0541) — inputs are never fabricated (D7).

ledger.text: Worst-of aggregation over evidence order violation < unclaimed < tested < fuzzed < bounded < proved (D6). Statuses (conditional, stale, weak-spec, unsupported, engine-missing, timeout, inconclusive) do not sit in that order — they propagate upward as flags and open-item counts alongside it.

This node's id is kept as 'ledger' for bundle stability (diagram node ids are stable keys); its label and every comment now use the current term, verdict tree (cargo ply tree, §6, §7). The concept and its worst-of aggregation (D6) are unchanged.

user.text: The developer or coding agent that runs cargo ply verify [path|fn] (§6) and receives the JSON envelope back. Ply's diagnostics are written for this reader either way — a human or an agent repairing code from a counterexample (§1 finding 2).

cli.text: ply-cli's verify entry point. It has no logic of its own here: it drives config load → anchor resolution → extraction → harness generation → engine run → aggregation in order and hands back whatever the verdict tree produces (§5.4–5.5, §7).

cfg.text: Loads and merges every ply.yaml and validates the result against the schema before anything else runs; a bad document fails fast with E0201/E0202/E0203 rather than reaching the engines (§5, §5.1).

model.text: Resolves each claim's anchor to a real code item (§5.2) and, once extraction returns facts, orders verification callees-before-callers over the call graph (§5.5) — the step that makes modular composition (D5) possible.

extract.text: Produces the item index, call graph, capability approximation, and anchors that model needs to build harnesses and check architecture rules; syn-based, so results are best-effort and every unresolved call site is still counted (D11, §5.3).

harness.text: Turns a resolved fn claim into runnable checking code: an in-crate Kani proof module, a proptest harness, or both, adding #[kani::stub_verified(g)] only when the callee already has its own passing proof this run (D5, §5.5). Also where the counterexample and Diagnostic get assembled once an engine reports back.

targetply.text: Where the generated proof modules and fuzz harnesses actually land, under target/ply/, entirely owned and cleaned up by Ply (§4, §6).

diag.text: Assembles the unified Diagnostic — code, span, counterexample, assumptions, fixes — from whatever the engine reported, then hands it to the verdict tree for aggregation (§8). Also the point where a rendered ply_cex_* test gets attached to the diagnostic when possible (D7).

generation.focus: The node tree workspace→components→fns (§7), the evidence order violation < unclaimed < tested < fuzzed < bounded < proved (D6), and the orthogonal statuses conditional/stale/weak-spec/unsupported/engine-missing/timeout/inconclusive (D6, §7). No code exists yet; modeled as a conceptual class diagram, left unanchored (files: []).

__diagram__.text: The model is a tree: workspace → components → nested components → fns (§7). Every node carries { id, kind, anchor, content_hash, verdict, statuses, worst_descendant, open_items }. Verdicts aggregate upward as worst-of over the evidence order (D6); statuses do not sit in that order — they propagate upward as flags and open-item counts alongside it (D6).

component.text: Components may nest (components: [...] with the same shape, §5.1) — omitted above as a self-loop for readability; a Component may contain further Components in addition to Fns.

node.text: node_id is the component path + item path only; content_hash (blake3) is a sibling field, never part of the id, so IDs survive edits (D10).

proved.text: Strongest evidence a function's passing checks can earn (§5.4c). A single failing check yields violation regardless of what else passed.

workspace.text: The root of the node tree: one per verify/tree run, carrying the command name and Ply version (§7). Everything else — components, nested components, fns — hangs underneath it.

fn.text: A leaf node: one function claim, its declared checks list (e.g. bounded(3), fuzz(256), mutate, §5.1/D12), and whether it runs in check or synth mode (§5.7). A fn's own verdict is the strongest evidence its passing checks earned — one failing check makes it a violation regardless (§5.4c).

violation.text: The weakest point on the evidence order: at least one check failed. A single failing check yields violation for the whole fn no matter what else passed (§5.4c, D6).

unclaimed.text: A node with no checks declared at all — weaker than any actual evidence, but not a failure (D6). This is the default state for a fn nobody has annotated yet.

tested.text: Verdict earned by the test check: example expressions from ply.yaml plus generated direct contract cases, run as concrete inputs through the real function (§5.4c).

fuzzed.text: Verdict earned by the fuzz(n) check: n proptest-generated inputs (default 256) with shrinking on; fuzzed(n) records how many cases actually ran (§5.4c).

bounded.text: Verdict earned by the bounded(k) check: a Kani contract proof exhaustive up to loop bound k (default 2) — every execution within the bound is checked, nothing is claimed beyond it (§0 'bounded model checking', §5.4c).

conditional.text: Attached when a fn's verification stubbed a callee whose own contract was merely assumed rather than proved this run — same crate but weaker evidence, cross-crate, or a call-graph cycle (D5, W0511). The verdict tree keeps the full assumption chain, not just the flag (§5.5).

stale.text: Attached when the recorded fingerprint no longer matches — item body, contract text, callee contracts, engine version, features, or target triple changed since the last accepted run (D14, W0302). cargo ply accept re-blesses it, but refuses (E0303) any node whose last run failed.

weak-spec.text: Attached when the mutate check finds surviving mutants: the spec verified but didn't actually constrain the mutated behavior (W0502, D12). The concrete defense against 'machine-written specs go vacuous' (§1 finding 4).

unsupported.text: Attached when an engine can't construct the fn's inputs at all — trait objects, generics, smart pointers, or a private-field type without a generator (§5.4b, V0505). Reported as a fact, never a harness build failure.

engine-missing.text: Attached when the engine a check needs isn't installed; the check is downgraded rather than the whole run failing (§3, W0110).

timeout.text: Attached when a check exceeds --engine-timeout (default 60s per fn, §6). Explicitly not treated as weaker evidence on the D6 order — it's a different kind of fact from a proof that ran to completion.

inconclusive.text: An orthogonal status for a check that ran but couldn't reach a definite pass/fail — kept separate from the evidence order (D6) so it's never confused with an actual weaker verdict.

kernel.text: Pure verdict kernel: evidence order, worst-of aggregation, status propagation (D5/D6). Four standing invariants proved exhaustively over 991,389 small trees by plain cargo test; Kani harnesses gated for symbolic proof. The renderer's ceiling fills call this real aggregate().

check.text: Document-local validator: E0203/E0205/E0206/E0304/E0504 plus W0409 (redundant parent-child edge). W-codes warn and exit 0; E-codes fail. Messages are plain-language and exact-string tested. Promoted into the product in Phase 1a (2026-08-25) together with the model: both now live in crates/ply-core and are what `cargo ply check` runs. `tools/check` is the binary and its CLI contract only, and it depends on ply-core by path.

render.text: The §7.1 visual grammar made literal: layered layout with routed polyline edges, collapse (--depth/--focus/--collapse) with stacked cards, hollow dashed boxes, declared-ceiling fills, contract marks, and red findings. Invariant tests walk the real SVG.

cargoply.text: The verification tool itself, and it exists now: `cargo ply` installs as a cargo subcommand with six commands — render, check, audit, worklist, verify, clean-views. render needs only the declaration file; check, audit and worklist are fast document-and-anchor passes with no engines; verify is the one that drives the engines and writes counterexample artifacts. Entry point crates/ply-cli/src/main.rs.

__diagram__.text: Current state of the tooling as of 2026-09-01. The 2026-08-23 version of this view split the work into "built" and "not built yet", with the actual verification tool on the unbuilt side; that split is gone because both halves now exist. The verdict kernel also moved: it is owned by the product (crates/ply-core/src/kernel.rs) and tools/kernel is a thin re-export kept so the older imports still compile. Everything here is checked in CI.

engines.text: Driven as subprocesses, never re-implemented. Kani for bounded proof, a generated proptest harness for fuzzing, cargo-mutants for mutation. crates/ply-core/src/engines/ holds one adapter per tool and crates/ply-core/src/schedule.rs orders the work callees-first, which is what makes a caller's credit honest.

edges.label: yes, clean all the way down

__diagram__.text: This walks the decisions Ply makes for ONE function claim that declares a `bounded` check -- the Kani-backed proof, and the only check kind where D5's three-branch split applies. A `fuzz` or `test` check on the same function skips the top decision entirely: it just runs the callee's real code, contract or not, so it never needs to stand in for anything. Left out on purpose: whether a previously recorded result can be reused instead of running any of this again -- that re-check, and what makes a stored result go unusable, is the subject of the companion state diagram (verdict-lifecycle), not this one.

scheduled.text: Before Ply checks a function, it first checks every function that function calls, within the same crate. It orders all of them so that a callee always gets its turn before its caller -- ties between two functions with no dependency on each other are broken by name, so re-running on unchanged code always produces the same order. A function stuck in a dependency cycle with another function -- or one that merely depends on something stuck in a cycle, however many calls away -- never gets a clean turn in this order at all, and falls straight through to "verify against an assumed promise" below for every contracted function it calls.

hascontract.text: A promise can be declared two ways: written directly on the callee's own function, or written separately for it in the project's `ply.yaml` file when the callee is old code nobody wants to annotate. Either counts as "has a contract" here. If neither exists, Ply will not open the callee's body to find out what it does -- see "Refuse To Descend" below. (Diagnostic W0512, described in section 5.5 of the spec.)

refuse.text: Ply will not silently read through code nobody has made a promise about, and it will not pretend the check ran anyway. The check earns nothing this run -- not a guess, not a partial credit, not a timeout -- and the verdict reads plainly as "nothing was checked." The warning that comes with it names the exact callee, and where in the caller's code it's called from, so this is something a person can actually go fix. It suggests two ways out: add a promise for the callee, or switch the check to `fuzz`, which crosses the same boundary by simply running the real code instead of needing a promise about it. Added 2026-08-25, closing a gap where a two-year-old, unannotated function used to just time out with no explanation instead.

proofpassed.text: "Already passed, clean" means the callee's own proof holds and that proof itself is not standing on some further unproven promise -- clean all the way down, not merely bounded-shaped. Everything else counts as "no" here: a callee that was only ever fuzz-tested or unit-tested, one that lives in a different crate, one that's part of a dependency cycle with this function, or one this run simply hasn't reached yet.

stubclean.text: Ply swaps the callee's real body out for a stand-in built purely from its promise, and checks the caller against that stand-in instead (Kani calls this stub_verified). Because the callee's own proof already held on its own, nothing here is being assumed -- but the result is only as deep as the shallower of the two: this function's own declared depth, or whatever depth the callee was actually proved to. A function declaring depth 5 that stands on a callee only proved to depth 2 gets a depth-2 result, never the deeper number.

assume.text: Ply still swaps in a stand-in for the callee, but this time the stand-in is built from a promise nobody has actually checked against the callee's real code yet. The result carries a visible mark saying it rests on an assumption, and that assumption itself is tracked as unproven debt until something runs the real callee against the same promise -- usually by fuzz-testing it. (Diagnostic W0511, section 5.5 of the spec.)

enginecheck.text: Every check Ply performs is actually carried out by a separate external tool -- Kani for a bounded proof, cargo-mutants for the mutation-testing tier. Before spending any time on the check itself, Ply confirms the tool is actually on the machine.

enginemissing.text: A missing tool is reported by name, with what to install -- never treated as a silent skip and never reported as though the check quietly passed. The check earns no evidence this run, and the run says exactly why.

runengine.text: Ply hands the work to the real tool and waits -- cargo kani for a bounded proof, the generated test harness for a fuzz or test check, cargo-mutants for the mutation tier -- until it finishes or runs out of its time budget.

parseresult.text: Ply strips out terminal colour codes before reading anything the tool printed -- a coloured "error:" line once slipped past every text match Ply had for it and was reported as an unattributable failure instead of the plain compiler error it actually was. Once the colour is gone, Ply reads the tool's own output closely enough to tell a genuine broken promise apart from the tool simply running out of time, crashing, or refusing to run at all -- three different facts that must never be reported as the same thing.

producevverdict.text: The final answer for this one check: how strong the evidence is (or that it's a genuine violation, or an honest "couldn't tell"), plus -- when a check actually found a case that breaks the promise -- the exact input that broke it. That input is kept as replayable data and, wherever it can be, is also turned into an ordinary test that fails on its own, so a person can see the failure without needing Ply at all.

__diagram__.text: This shows the states one claim's verdict can occupy across runs, and the event that moves it from one to another. It deliberately does not repeat the shape of a verdict node itself (fields, types, statuses as data) -- that is already drawn in this bundle's class diagram, verdict-model. It also does not show how several checks declared on the same function combine into one reported verdict; that is an implementation detail, not a lifecycle state. Two things worth naming plainly: first, the kernel's own evidence scale has a strongest rung above Bounded called Proved, but nothing in Ply can earn it today -- the check that would produce it (`prove`) has no engine behind it yet, so this diagram stops at Bounded rather than drawing a state nothing can reach. Second, the tool's rendering code still carries a leftover `Stale` status it knows how to draw, from an earlier design -- but nothing anywhere in the checking pipeline ever actually sets it any more, matching the current spec's own claim that there is no stale state: a claim whose recorded answer no longer matches simply gets re-checked from scratch, which is what the loop back to "No Evidence Yet" below shows instead.

noevidence.text: This is where every claim starts, and it is also exactly what "unclaimed" means everywhere else in Ply: a claim nobody has answered yet, and a claim Ply refused to check (because a callee it needed to look through had no promise attached) both read identically -- there is no separate "refused" state.

tested.text: Earned when the function declares a `test` check and its worked examples all hold. This is one rung above having no evidence at all, and one rung below Fuzzed.

fuzzed.text: Earned when the function declares `fuzz(n)` and every one of the n generated cases holds. Stronger than Tested (more cases, generated rather than hand-written), weaker than Bounded (sampled, not exhaustive).

bounded.text: Earned when a `bounded(k)` check is proved exhaustively up to size k, either directly or by standing cleanly on a callee's own already-passed proof (in which case the reported depth is capped at whichever is shallower: this function's own declared depth, or the callee's proved depth). This is the strongest evidence Ply can currently earn -- the kernel's evidence scale defines one rung above it, Proved, but no check today has an engine behind it that can produce that rung.

resting.text: The claim still earned Tested, Fuzzed, or Bounded evidence at whatever strength its check produced -- this mark rides alongside that evidence rather than replacing it, because standing on an unproven promise doesn't erase what was otherwise checked. It's reached whenever the callee being stood on wasn't itself clean this run: merely fuzz- or unit-tested, living in a different crate, caught in a dependency cycle, or simply not checked yet. The moment this mark is set, the assumption behind it is also tracked as unpaid debt.

discharged.text: The "resting on an assumption" mark itself never goes away while the proof is still standing on a promise instead of the callee's real body -- only the debt half clears, once something has actually run the real callee against that same promise (typically by fuzz-testing it) and it held. `cargo ply audit` and `cargo ply worklist` are what track this debt in the meantime, from two different angles: audit lists it as permanent trust surface, worklist lists it as work that can still be closed.

violation.text: The weakest result there is -- weaker even than having no evidence at all. Found when a check turns up a concrete case where the code breaks its own promise. A violation anywhere drags everything containing it down to a violation too, no matter how much else nearby was cleanly proved.

__diagram__.text: Shows every artifact cargo-ply reads, generates, or writes, and how data moves between them, across all five subcommands (render, check, audit, worklist, verify). It deliberately leaves out the verdict kernel's internal computation -- that is how results are combined, not what moves between files, and it leaves out the exact shape of one diagnostic (the JSON envelope's own fields do that job). ply.lock and the generated harnesses only ever appear when `cargo ply verify` runs; render, check, audit and worklist read only the declaration file, plus -- for check, audit and worklist -- the crate's own Rust source, just to confirm each anchor resolves to real code.

yaml.text: The declaration file a user writes by hand: which components exist, which function each one makes a promise about, and what that promise is. Ply reads this file's text before touching any Rust source, and rejects an unsupported `ply:` schema version before parsing goes any further (crates/ply-core/src/config.rs:69-87, `load`/`load_str`, code E0201). The repo's own ply.yaml and vetting/003-trading-system.ply.yaml are real examples of this file.

schema.text: The JSON Schema that fixes the declaration file's grammar -- which keys are allowed and what shape their values take -- rather than the Rust parser deciding that on its own. It is compiled straight into the cargo-ply binary at build time (crates/ply-core/src/schema.rs:28, `include_str!("../../../schema/ply.schema.json")`), so there is exactly one copy of the grammar, never two that could disagree. A typo'd key is checked against it and reported with the nearest real key name before the file is even parsed into a document (crates/ply-core/src/config.rs:51-62, code E0204).

document.text: The in-memory tree every Ply command actually works with, built by parsing ply.yaml's text (crates/ply-core/src/config.rs:77-86, `load_str`). It holds the component tree, each function's promises, the call and data-flow edges, and the architecture ban rules -- see the declaration-grammar diagram for its full shape. `render`, `check`, `audit` and `worklist` stop here and never invoke a compiler or an external tool; only `verify` goes further and reads real source too.

source.text: The real .rs files of whatever crate ply.yaml's `anchor:` fields point at -- when Ply checks itself, that is Ply's own crates. `cargo ply check` reads the crate's src/lib.rs to confirm every anchor actually resolves to real code (crates/ply-cli/src/check.rs:332, `std::fs::read_to_string(&lib_path)`), and `verify` reads the same source again to find each promised function's exact body, so it can turn that body into a proof or a test (crates/ply-core/src/harness.rs, the harness codegen). The files listed on this node are the Ply code that does the reading, not the source being read -- that varies by project.

lock.text: The committed record of every result Ply has already earned, one entry per checked function, each stored beside a fingerprint hash of everything that result depended on -- the function's own source, its declared promises, the callees it stands on, and more (crates/ply-core/src/record.rs:96-140 lists the exact inputs by name). `verify` reads it at the start of a run (crates/ply-cli/src/verify.rs:398-399, `crate_dir.join("ply.lock")`) and, for each function, recomputes today's fingerprint: a match reuses the old result untouched, a mismatch runs the check again. The file is rewritten at the end of every run (crates/ply-cli/src/verify.rs:1288) so the next run starts from today's answers. tests/fixtures/paramseedopaque/ply.lock is a real example of one.

verify_engine.text: The part of `cargo ply verify` that actually runs a check: it decides, per function, whether Kani (a bounded proof), proptest (randomised fuzzing), or cargo-mutants applies, and drives whichever one is needed (crates/ply-cli/src/verify.rs). It is the only place in Ply that runs an external tool against generated code -- render, check, audit and worklist never do, which is exactly why those four commands run in a fraction of a second and this one can take minutes.

proof_harness.text: A Kani proof, generated from one function's promises and written straight into the checked crate's own src/ply_generated.rs, with a `mod ply_generated;` line added to its lib.rs if one isn't already there (crates/ply-core/src/harness.rs:4085-4114, `write_generated_module`/`write_generated_file`). Writing it inside the crate rather than off to the side is deliberate: it lets the generated proof see private items the crate never exports. tests/fixtures/vecbound/src/ply_generated.rs is a real example left on disk from an earlier fixture run.

cex_test.text: An ordinary #[test], generated only when a proof or a fuzz run actually finds an input that breaks a promise, and written into the checked crate as src/ply_generated_cex.rs the same way as the proof harness (crates/ply-core/src/harness.rs:4098-4114, `write_generated_test`; called from crates/ply-cli/src/verify.rs:1219). It replays the exact failing input Kani or proptest found, so a developer can rerun `cargo test` and see the same failure without invoking Ply again. No example is checked into this repo because it only exists for the length of a run that actually found a violation.

fuzz_crate.text: A separate, disposable Cargo crate that Ply writes under the checked crate's own target/ply/fuzz/<name>/ (crates/ply-core/src/harness_crate.rs:146-149, `harness_rel_path`), holding the generated property tests for the `fuzz`/`test` checks and whatever `mutate` needs to run cargo-mutants against. It is a separate crate, not a file inside the checked crate, because these checks need their own Cargo.toml and a dependency on proptest; the module comment at the top of harness_crate.rs explains the two different ways it gets wired into the checked crate's own workspace.

svg.text: The picture `cargo ply render` produces: every component as a box, every call and data-flow edge as an arrow (crates/ply-core/src/visual/svg.rs). It needs only the declaration file to draw -- no compiler, no engines -- so it can draw a document `check` would refuse. Printed to stdout by default, or written to a file with -o (crates/ply-cli/src/main.rs, the final branch of `render_command_with_format`). vetting/003-trading-system.svg is a real rendered example.

text.text: The --text output of `cargo ply render`: the same facts as the SVG, written out as prose instead of drawn, including a few details the drawing only shows on hover (crates/ply-core/src/visual/transcript.rs). Meant for a terminal, a pipe, or a model -- none of which can hover over an SVG. vetting/003-trading-system-full.txt is a real example.

json_envelope.text: The machine-readable report any command can produce with the global --json flag: one diagnostic per finding, each with a verdict, its evidence, and a stable code (crates/ply-core/src/diag.rs, `Envelope`/`to_json_pretty`). `check`, `audit` and `worklist` fill it in from the declaration file and the resolved anchors alone, in well under a second; `verify` fills the same shape in from what the engines actually found (crates/ply-cli/src/main.rs, the `cli.json` branch under each subcommand). It always goes to stdout -- there is no file output for this report.

visual_snapshot.text: A frozen combination of the declared picture and one completed `verify` run's outcome, written only when --publish-view is passed (crates/ply-cli/src/main.rs:248-257). It lands at target/ply/views/<run-id>/visual.json, one folder per run, with target/ply/view.json as the index every editor client reads first to find the current run (crates/ply-core/src/visual/mod.rs:764-769, 796-839). `cargo ply clean-views` prunes older runs from this index without touching the current one (crates/ply-core/src/visual/mod.rs:873). This lets an editor extension show live results without ever parsing ply.yaml or running engines itself.

__diagram__.text: Shows the entities a ply.yaml declaration file is actually built from, in the parsed form crates/ply-core/src/model.rs defines, and how they relate. It deliberately leaves out the three engines that check these promises (Kani, proptest, cargo-mutants -- see the dataflow diagram) and the verdict kernel that combines their results; this diagram is only about what a user writes and what it turns into in memory, not what happens to it afterward. `anchor` -- a component's link to real code -- is drawn as a plain string field on Component here, not as its own entity: the code has no separate struct for it, only a resolver function that either finds the code it names or reports that it couldn't.

document.text: The whole declaration file, parsed into one tree (crates/ply-core/src/model.rs:19-38, `struct Document`). `ply: 1` is the only schema version this build accepts -- anything else is refused before the rest of the file is even read (crates/ply-core/src/config.rs:80-85, code E0201). `components` and `externals` preserve the order they were written in (an IndexMap, not a sorted map), so a rendered drawing lists things in the same order a human reading the file would.

component.text: One named unit of the checked codebase -- usually a crate or a module -- declared under `components:` (crates/ply-core/src/model.rs:44-89, `struct Component`). `anchor` is the one field with no default: it names the real crate or module path this component actually is, and an anchor nobody's code matches is reported as E0301. `pure`, `strict`, `uses` and `owns` are architecture rules -- which capabilities a component may use, which types only it may touch; `checks` is a default every function inside it inherits unless it declares its own (a fn's own list always replaces the inherited one rather than joining it -- an empty list on purpose means "check nothing here", which is a different statement from declaring no list at all). `components` nests further components the same shape, so the tree can be as deep as the codebase it describes.

fnclaim.text: One promise about one function, declared under a component's `fns:` map and keyed by that function's name (crates/ply-core/src/model.rs:111-133, `struct FnClaim`). `requires`/`ensures` are the actual contract text an engine attacks; `examples` are worked test cases; `check_with` fills in a generic type parameter so a proof has a concrete type to reason about. `entry` names which declared externals are allowed to call into this function, which turns its `requires` into an assumption about the environment rather than something the caller must prove -- it changes what a reader sees, never the verdict itself.

check.text: One entry from a checks: list -- either a component's default or a function's own -- parsed from one of five literal spellings (crates/ply-core/src/model.rs:252-322, `enum Check`/`parse_check`): test, fuzz(N), bounded(K), prove, or mutate. fuzz's count is how many random inputs get tried (1 to 1,000,000); bounded's count is how many times a loop gets unrolled during the proof (1 to 64) -- both refuse an out-of-range or malformed number with a plain-language reason rather than a bare parse error.

external.text: An outside party this codebase talks to but Ply never verifies -- a payment processor, an exchange, a person -- declared under the top-level externals: map, keyed by name (crates/ply-core/src/model.rs:97-101, `struct External`). Its note is required rather than optional: an external is nothing but a name and a sentence, and a bare name with no explanation tells a reader nothing about what it is or why it's trusted.

profile.text: A named, reusable set of architecture bans, declared once under the document's top-level profiles: map and opted into by any component's own profile: field (crates/ply-core/src/model.rs:37, `Document.profiles`; schema/ply.schema.json's `profiles`/`profile` properties). `bans` is a list of names drawn from a fixed vocabulary the schema defines (crates/ply-core/src/schema.rs:199-200, `fn bans`). vetting/003-trading-system.ply.yaml declares `hot_path: [no_panics, exhaustive_match]` and its `ring` and `decoder` components opt into it by name.

edge.text: One relationship line from the document's edges: list, parsed from one of two micro-syntaxes (crates/ply-core/src/model.rs:333-388, `struct Edge`/`parse_edge`): "a -> b" means a may call b, "a ~> b : Type" means data of that type actually flows from a to b. `from` and `to` are plain names, each naming either a declared component (by its dotted path) or a declared external -- vetting/003-trading-system.ply.yaml's "gateway ~> venue : FixMessage" is a real example naming an external on the right-hand side.

deny.text: One architecture ban from the document's deny: list, parsed as "a -> b" or "a -> b except c, d" (crates/ply-core/src/model.rs:391-420, `struct Deny`/`parse_deny`). Either side may be a literal component name or the wildcard *, and `except` lists specific names the ban does not apply to. A violated deny rule is what makes an architecture check fail -- it is the one rule in this grammar written as a negative.

trusted.text: One human assertion a function's contract stands on instead of an engine's proof -- "this was checked some other way, and here's where" -- declared under a function's trusted: list (crates/ply-core/src/model.rs:203-207, `struct TrustedClaim`). `evidence` is free text naming where that other checking happened (a test file, an audit, a certification run); Ply reads it and shows it, but never verifies the claim itself -- that is the whole point of the word "trusted".

unresolved.text: One open question the author has recorded rather than answered -- "we haven't decided this yet, and here's what's undecided" -- with a stable numeric id so it can be referenced elsewhere and a note explaining it (crates/ply-core/src/model.rs:210-214, `struct UnresolvedEntry`). It can appear at the top of the whole document or on a single function's own unresolved: list, wherever the open question actually belongs.

__diagram__.text: How Ply actually runs the tools that check a function's promises. Ply is one single-threaded process: there is no thread pool, no async runtime, and no sign anywhere in the codebase of two things running at once (checked directly: grepping every crate under crates/*/src for thread::spawn, tokio, rayon, and channel types such as std::sync::mpsc turns up nothing). Ply drives one loop that checks one function at a time, and inside that loop it spawns exactly one external tool at a time -- Kani, the fuzz harness's tests, or cargo-mutants -- and blocks until that tool exits before doing anything else (the fuzz and mutants runs go through one blocking helper, `engines::run_with_timeout`, which spawns the child, polls for its exit on the same thread, and kills it if its wall-clock budget runs out; the Kani proof run is a plain blocking `Command::new(...).output()`, with Kani's own `--harness-timeout` flag as its cap -- either way, one child at a time, nothing concurrent). The order the loop checks functions in is decided by a callees-before-callers rule (crates/ply-core/src/schedule.rs), not by a scheduler trying to go faster: a function can only be credited with its callee's result once that callee has genuinely been checked, so getting the order wrong would let a caller claim evidence its callee never actually earned. That is a soundness requirement -- the same kind of rule this project's own verdict-kernel proof protects elsewhere -- not a performance optimisation. Left out of this picture on purpose: the short version-probe calls to rustc and cargo-mutants (they answer 'which version is installed', not part of the checking work itself), and the fact that cargo kani / cargo test / cargo mutants are each free to use their own internal build parallelism once Ply has started them -- that happens inside the child process, is invisible to Ply, and is not what this diagram is about.

ply-verify.text: Ply itself: the single process a developer or CI job starts by running `cargo ply verify`. Everything else in this diagram happens inside this one process, on its one thread, one step after another -- there is no background work happening anywhere else.

verify-loop.text: The loop, inside the Ply process, that checks each function one at a time (`for idx in processing_order`, crates/ply-cli/src/verify.rs:1162). Before it starts, `ply_core::schedule::order` works out which order to go in: callees are checked before the callers that depend on them, because a caller may only be credited with an assumed contract if its callee's own check already passed cleanly (crates/ply-core/src/schedule.rs's module comment spells this out as the scheduler's entire soundness guarantee). When one function has more than one kind of check -- say both a bounded check and a mutation check -- even those two run one after the other, never together: the mutation check deliberately waits until the other check's result is known before it starts (crates/ply-cli/src/verify.rs:2586).

harness-files.text: The small generated test crate Ply writes for the function currently being checked -- a Cargo.toml plus a lib.rs, placed at `<crate>/target/ply/fuzz/<name>` (crates/ply-core/src/harness_crate.rs). Ply writes these files before it spawns any checking tool for that function, and every tool it then spawns builds and runs against exactly these files -- they are the common ground every tool's result is actually about.

workspace-manifest.text: The Cargo.toml belonging to the crate being checked, not to Ply. Ply temporarily adds the generated harness to this file's list of workspace members for the whole verify run so cargo can find and build it, then writes the original file back once the run ends (the `ManifestRegistration` guard, crates/ply-core/src/harness_crate.rs:239-312). Every tool Ply spawns needs this edit in place to resolve the harness package at all -- it is genuinely shared, mutated state, not just a read-only input.

cargo-kani.text: Kani, the model checker, spawned as its own process: `cargo kani -Z function-contracts ... --harness <name>` (crates/ply-core/src/engines/kani.rs:135-151). Ply waits for it to finish and reads all of its output before doing anything else. It answers the `bounded` check: does the function hold up against every input Kani can enumerate up to a size limit, not just the ones a test happened to try.

cargo-fuzz.text: `cargo test -p <harness>`, spawned the same blocking way as every other engine here, its wall-clock budget enforced in-process by `engines::run_with_timeout` -- never by an external `timeout` binary, which macOS does not ship (crates/ply-core/src/engines/fuzz.rs:43-83). It runs the generated harness's randomised test cases -- built on the `proptest` library -- to answer the `fuzz` check.

cargo-mutants.text: cargo-mutants, spawned as `cargo mutants -p <crate> --test-package <harness> --copy-target true ...`, with the whole invocation's wall-clock cap enforced in-process by `engines::run_with_timeout` -- never by an external `timeout` wrapper (crates/ply-core/src/engines/mutants.rs:152-215). It deliberately breaks the checked function one small way at a time and reruns the harness's tests, to see whether any of those breakages go unnoticed -- the `mutate` check. `--copy-target true` exists because of a real bug this project found and documented: cargo-mutants' own tree-copy step silently skips any directory literally named `target` sitting at the very top of what it is copying, and that is exactly where the generated harness lives, one level further down (crates/ply-core/src/engines/mutants.rs's own top-of-file comment).

mutants-out.text: `mutants.out/`, the folder cargo-mutants writes its results into. Ply deletes any copy left over from an earlier run before spawning cargo-mutants, so an old run's files can never be mistaken for this run's, then reads the fresh files back afterwards to count which mutations were caught, missed, or timed out (crates/ply-core/src/engines/mutants.rs:174-196).
